messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lani, a 20-year-old Māori and Samoan woman who worked as an interior designer, came to treatment after months of feeling as though ordinary life had narrowed around one violent relationship. The abuse had come from her husband, a man she had once trusted completely. What finally made the event feel unforgettable was the unpredictability of it: an argument in their apartment escalated when he shoved her against the wall, grabbed her hard enough to leave bruises, and shouted over a slammed door that made her ears ring. Afterward, even small reminders seemed to carry the force of that night. A sudden bang in a client’s home, a heavy cabinet door in the studio, or being left alone in a room with a man she did not know well could make her body brace before she had time to think. She began arranging site visits so a coworker would go with her, avoiding dark stairwells, empty parking areas, and any circumstance that felt like being trapped in the same helplessness. She said that when she was near men she did not know, she watched their hands and shoulders, and if she ever heard loud noises she felt her whole body spring into readiness, as if danger were about to strike again.

What stayed most alive for Lani was not a neat story she could tell, but fragments that came with missing pieces. When she tried to explain what had happened, she would lose the thread partway through, staring down and starting over, unable to finish. At other times, remembering the abuse brought a wave of guilt so intense that she felt she deserved it for not leaving sooner. Sometimes the memory arrived differently, as a sudden rush of terror and shame with no clear image attached, only the bodily certainty that she was back in danger. Those moments made her scan the room immediately, and she often found herself looking behind her, checking doorways and reflections to see whether someone was following her. The memory of the assault also fed the meanings she had begun to attach to her life: she had come to believe her life had been destroyed by what happened, that she no longer belonged anywhere, and that people could not be trusted. Those beliefs made every startled glance and guarded explanation feel reasonable to her, because if others were unsafe and her own life had already been ruined, she could not afford to be careless.

Over the following weeks, Lani’s efforts to manage the fear gradually shaped the world around it. She avoided being alone in a room or building, and at work she found herself taking the long way through the studio rather than crossing quiet corridors or entering a darkened storage area. She kept lights on whenever she could and became uneasy in dim spaces, as if darkness itself might hide another blow. The more she arranged her days around not being caught unprepared, the smaller and more controlled her routines became. That vigilance brought a momentary sense of safety, but it also kept her body tense and ready to react, and the strain of staying watchful all day left her exhausted. She checked behind her repeatedly when walking from her car or leaving a client meeting, and the habit made every ordinary sound feel more suspicious, especially loud noises that could have been a slam or a strike. Those same moments also pulled the memory closer, and once the memory surfaced, the guilt and conviction that her life had been ruined returned with it. In turn, she withdrew even further, convinced that staying away from circumstances that reminded her of the abuse was the only way to avoid being hurt again.

By the time she sought help, Lani described a life organized around avoiding reminders, scanning for threat, and enduring periods when the whole emotional force of the assault returned without warning. She was most afraid that the fear had become permanent, that she would never again feel safe with people or in her own home. What brought her in was the realization that the same strategies meant to protect her were now keeping her stuck: she was isolating herself from her husband, from coworkers, and from the ordinary confidence she needed to do her job. She hoped treatment might help her stop feeling constantly on guard and find a way to remember what happened without being flooded by guilt and terror, even though part of her still feared that trusting anyone, including the therapist, would only prove her right about people.
